description: We are a diverse team of four individuals from different backgrounds — education, retirement, accounting, and IT — brought together by our shared curiosity and passion for learning. Despite our different experiences and skill sets, we unite to explore science, STEM, and AI through the NASA Space Apps Challenge. We believe everyone has something valuable to contribute, and together, we turn different perspectives into creative ideas with the hope of making a positive difference in the world.
summary: Space Relics: The Forgotten Footprints of Space Exploration is an interactive educational web platform that explores human-made equipment left behind on the Moon and Mars throughout the history of space exploration. Through interactive planetary maps, historical photographs, mission timelines, and detailed equipment profiles, users can discover where these objects are located, why they were left behind, and the important roles they played in their respective missions. The platform aims to transform scattered historical information into an engaging digital museum, making space exploration history more accessible to students, educators, and space enthusiasts. By highlighting the stories and scientific contributions of these forgotten objects, Space Relics encourages users to appreciate humanity's journey beyond Earth and recognize that every space mission leaves behind a story worth remembering.

Space Relics: The Forgotten Footprints of Space Exploration

Live website: https://lynn2160-dev.github.io/space-relics/Source code: https://github.com/lynn2160-dev/space-relics

Space Relics: The Forgotten Footprints of Space Exploration is an educational website about the human-made equipment left on the Moon and Mars, and the stories behind each piece. It has three main parts:

  • Interactive maps of the Moon and Mars, built on NASA global mosaics (the LRO Wide Angle Camera mosaic for the Moon and the Viking colorized mosaic for Mars). Each landing site has a marker, and clicking it opens that object's story.
  • Six equipment stories: the Apollo 11 descent stage, the Lunar Roving Vehicle, the ALSEP science instruments, Surveyor 3, Sojourner, and Spirit. Each story covers what the object is, where it is, why it was left behind, what it contributed, and where the facts come from.
  • A searchable archive that can be filtered by world, mission, and equipment type, and sorted.

A "Method & Sources" section explains how the objects were chosen, where the facts come from, and who took each image.

What are the benefits?

  • Scattered knowledge is gathered in one place. Information about lunar and Martian hardware is usually spread across mission pages, history books, and technical reports. Space Relics puts it together and explains it in plain language.
  • Readers learn by place. Seeing where each object sits on a real NASA map makes the history easier to picture and remember.
  • Every claim can be checked. Each story lists its sources, so students and teachers can go to the original NASA material.
  • Anyone can use it. It runs in any browser on desktop or mobile, supports keyboard navigation, and needs no account or installation.

What is the intended impact?

  • We want people to see these objects as evidence of human ingenuity, scientific discovery, and the hard trade-offs of exploration, not as junk. Our tagline is "Not debris. Evidence." The site is meant to spark curiosity in students and the public, support classroom teaching, and encourage people to think about these sites as part  of humanity's shared heritage, something worth remembering and possibly protecting as more missions head back to the Moon and Mars.

What tools, languages, hardware, or software did we use?

  • Languages: JavaScript (JSX), HTML, CSS
  • Frameworks and libraries: React 18, Vite 6, Leaflet with React Leaflet for the maps
  • Data and imagery: NASA mission pages, NASA history publications, NASA technical reports, the LRO WAC global Moon mosaic, the Viking MDIM 2.1 colorized Mars mosaic, and NASA archive photographs
  • Development tools: Node.js and npm, Git and GitHub, with GitHub Pages for hosting (live at https://lynn2160-dev.github.io/space-relics/)
  • Hardware: a standard laptop. The site is frontend only, with no backend, database, or server costs.

How is the project creative?

  • It treats space hardware like museum artifacts. The "atlas" design pairs real planetary maps with archive-style cards and a story view.
  • The interface is built around storytelling, not data tables. Each object gets a short narrative with a headline that answers the human questions: why was it left there, and what did it give us?
  • It covers two worlds in one shared history, linking crewed Apollo hardware and robotic Mars rovers as chapters of the same story.
  • The visual design is custom: an illustrated lunar hero, orbit lines, and coordinate labels that make the site feel like an exploration log.

What factors did our team consider?

  • Accuracy: we used only NASA primary and official sources, and each story cites its own. Map coordinates come from published landing-site data and are labeled as approximate, for education only.
  • Variety: the six objects cover the main kinds of hardware left behind: a crewed landing stage, a crewed vehicle, surface science instruments, a robotic lander, and two Mars rovers.
  • Licensing and credit: all imagery follows NASA media guidelines and is fully credited, with a clear note that NASA does not endorse the project.
  • Accessibility and reach: the layout works on mobile, supports keyboard navigation, uses descriptive labels, and shows a placeholder if a remote photo fails to load so the story text is always available.
  • Simplicity and sustainability: a frontend-only design means no running costs, easy hosting, and easy updates. All story text lives in one data file, so adding a new relic is straightforward.
  • Scope: we started with six well-documented objects so each story could be done carefully, and built the structure so more objects can be added later.
